passages.q: Why might deciding where cash goes be a CEO’s most important job?
p: Over a long tenure, the chief executive of a profitable company will deploy far more capital than the company was worth when they began, choosing repeatedly among reinvesting in existing operations, acquiring other businesses, paying down debt, paying dividends and buying back shares; because the returns on these choices compound, differences in allocation skill can produce enormous differences in long-run value, even between companies with similar operating performance.

The writer William Thorndike, studying chief executives whose companies delivered exceptional long-term returns, highlighted Henry Singleton of Teledyne, who in the 1960s used his company’s richly valued shares to acquire dozens of businesses and then, when the shares became cheap in the 1970s, reversed course and bought back a large proportion of them. Singleton’s distinguishing trait was not a fixed preference for any one use of cash but a disciplined willingness to compare the expected returns of all of them, including doing nothing, and to act against prevailing fashion when the numbers demanded it.

The lesson cuts against common practice. Many companies pursue growth for its own sake, acquiring at high prices because scale is admired, or buy back shares when they are expensive because cash is plentiful, and fewer explicitly compare the return on each option with its cost. A useful discipline for any executive is to ask, of every significant use of capital, what return it is expected to earn per pound invested and whether that beats the best available alternative, including handing the money back to shareholders.
g: A long-serving CEO deploys more capital than the firm was worth, so compounding allocation choices create huge value differences.
Singleton used expensive shares to buy firms then bought shares back when cheap, because he compared all options’ returns against fashion.
Many firms chase growth or buy back at high prices, so executives should compare each use of capital’s return with the best alternative.
k: CEOs allocate more capital over time than the firm’s starting value; allocation skill compounds.
Singleton issued expensive shares for acquisitions, then bought back cheap shares, comparing all options.
Ask of every capital use: expected return per pound versus the best alternative, including returning cash.

passages.q: How can a company with growing revenue be losing more money with every customer?
p: Headline revenue can mislead, because it says nothing about whether each additional sale makes the business better or worse off. Unit economics asks that question directly: for a single unit of the business, whether an order, a customer or a subscription, what revenue does it bring in, what variable costs does it consume, and what is left, the contribution margin, to cover fixed costs and generate profit? A company whose contribution margin is negative loses more money the more it sells, however impressive its growth.

Several high-profile start-ups in the 2010s, particularly in on-demand delivery and ride-hailing, grew rapidly while subsidising each transaction, on the theory that scale would eventually improve the economics through density, better routing or reduced incentives. In some cases it did; in others, once subsidies were removed, customers left, revealing that demand had depended on prices below cost. The distinction between businesses whose unit economics improve with scale and those that merely grow is among the most important judgements an investor or strategist can make.

Calculating unit economics honestly requires care. Costs that appear fixed may rise with volume in steps, such as warehouses or support staff; acquisition costs must be compared with the lifetime value of a customer, which depends on retention assumptions that are easy to flatter; and averages can conceal segments that are deeply unprofitable. The aim is to know, with evidence rather than optimism, whether the next unit sold creates value or destroys it.
g: Revenue hides whether each sale helps, so unit economics measures contribution per unit, and negative margins lose more with growth.
Subsidised start-ups grew fast hoping scale would fix economics, which sometimes worked and sometimes collapsed when subsidies ended.
Honest calculation must watch step costs, flattering retention assumptions and hidden unprofitable segments to know if each unit creates value.
k: Unit economics asks what each unit contributes after variable costs; negative contribution worsens with growth.
Subsidised growth sometimes improved with scale and sometimes collapsed when subsidies ended.
Watch step costs, retention assumptions and unprofitable segments; know if the next unit creates value.

passages.q: How can the timing of cash make a company stronger than its profits suggest?
p: Profit and cash are not the same thing. A company records revenue when it makes a sale, but it may not be paid for weeks; it may hold inventory for months before selling it; and it may itself pay suppliers on delay. The cash conversion cycle combines these intervals, the days inventory is held plus the days customers take to pay minus the days the company takes to pay its suppliers, to measure how long cash is tied up in the business between paying for inputs and collecting from customers.

A short or negative cycle can be a powerful advantage. Dell, in the 1990s, built computers to order, held very little inventory, collected payment from customers quickly by card and paid its suppliers later, so that at times it was effectively financed by its suppliers and customers: it received cash before it had to pay for the components. Amazon’s retail business benefited from a similar dynamic as it grew, since rising sales generated cash rather than consuming it, funding expansion without heavy borrowing.

Long cycles, by contrast, mean that growth consumes cash, since each additional sale requires financing inventory and receivables before money comes in, and many profitable but fast-growing companies have failed because they ran out of cash rather than profits. For executives, the cycle is often an underused lever: negotiating payment terms, reducing inventory and speeding collection can release large amounts of cash without any change in sales or margins, which is why finance teams examine working capital as closely as profit.
g: Profit differs from cash, and the cash conversion cycle measures how long cash is tied up from paying for inputs to collecting from customers.
Short or negative cycles are an advantage, as Dell and Amazon were paid before paying suppliers, funding growth.
Long cycles make growth consume cash and sink profitable firms, so terms, inventory and collection are powerful levers.

passages.q: Why do customers stay with products they would not choose today?
p: Switching costs are the expenses, efforts and risks a customer bears when changing from one supplier to another, and they include far more than any explicit fee: retraining staff on new software, migrating data, rewriting integrations with other systems, renegotiating contracts, losing accumulated history or loyalty rewards, and the uncertainty of whether the alternative will work as promised. Where these costs are high, customers may remain with a product even when a rival is better or cheaper.

Enterprise software illustrates the effect vividly. Once a company has built its finance, customer or design workflows around a particular system, with years of files, templates and trained staff, the cost of moving can exceed the cost of the product itself by a wide margin, which allows established vendors to raise prices or to maintain them in the face of cheaper competitors. Investors therefore value high switching costs as a source of durable advantage, and companies often design products to deepen them, by encouraging customers to store more data or adopt more connected features.

Switching costs are a double-edged asset. Customers who stay because they feel trapped rather than satisfied may resent the vendor and leave as soon as the barrier falls, for example when a new standard, open data format or regulation lowers the cost of moving, and competitors may target exactly those disgruntled users with migration tools and incentives. The most durable position combines switching costs with genuine continuing value, so that customers stay because leaving would be costly and because staying is still worth it.
g: Switching costs include retraining, data migration, integrations, lost history and uncertainty, so customers may stay despite better rivals.
Enterprise software shows moving can cost more than the product, letting vendors hold prices, so firms deepen these costs.
Trapped customers resent vendors and leave when barriers fall, so durable positions combine switching costs with real value.
k: Switching costs include retraining, migration, integrations, lost history and risk.

passages.q: What does it mean for a business to have pricing power, and why is it so valuable?
p: Warren Buffett has said that, when judging a business, few questions matter more than whether it can put up prices without customers drifting to competitors, and that a business which agonises over even a modest rise is in a weak position; the point captures, in a sentence, what formal strategy frameworks approach more laboriously: the ability to set price is the clearest evidence of a durable advantage.

Pricing power arises when customers have few acceptable alternatives or when what they would lose by switching outweighs the price difference, whether because of brand, network effects, switching costs, regulation or a product that is a small but critical part of the customer’s costs. That last source is often underappreciated: a component that represents a tiny fraction of a buyer’s total spending but whose failure would be costly can sustain high prices, since buyers rarely risk the whole to save on the part.

Its value shows most clearly during inflation. Companies with pricing power can pass rising costs on to customers and protect their margins, while those without it see profits squeezed between suppliers and buyers. Pricing power is not, however, a licence to extract indefinitely; prices set far above the value delivered invite competitors, regulation and resentment, and the most enduring firms tend to use their power sparingly, raising prices in line with the value they add rather than simply because they can.
g: Buffett argues the key factor in judging a business is whether it can raise prices without losing customers, the clearest sign of advantage.
Pricing power comes from few alternatives or high switching losses, including small but critical components buyers will not risk.

passages.q: Why do so many acquisitions fail to create the value promised?
p: Acquisitions are announced with confident projections of synergies, cost savings from combining operations and revenue gains from cross-selling, yet a large body of research over several decades suggests that many fail to create value for the acquiring company’s shareholders, with studies often finding that the acquirer’s share price, on average, does not rise and frequently falls when a deal is announced, while the target’s shareholders capture most of the gains.

Several forces contribute. In competitive bidding, the winner tends to be the most optimistic bidder, so the price often embeds overestimated synergies; revenue synergies in particular are easy to promise and hard to deliver. Integration absorbs management attention for years and frequently encounters clashes of culture, systems and incentives that projections ignore, while key staff and customers of the acquired company may leave during the upheaval. And chief executives may pursue deals partly because size brings status and pay, a principal-agent problem that boards do not always check.

Successful acquirers tend to share disciplined habits: they pay prices justified by realistic synergies rather than by strategic enthusiasm, favour smaller, related deals they can integrate repeatedly over transformational bets, plan integration before the deal closes, and walk away when bidding escalates. The question to ask of any proposed acquisition is not whether the combined company would be attractive, but whether the price paid leaves enough of the value for the buyer once the costs and risks of combination are honestly counted.
g: Deals promise synergies, but research suggests many fail to create value for acquirers, whose share prices often fall while targets gain.

passages.t: Most of the value is in the far future
passages.q: Why can a valuation model be dominated by assumptions about distant years?
p: A discounted cash flow valuation estimates a company’s worth by forecasting the cash it will generate in future years and converting those amounts into present values using a discount rate that reflects risk and the time value of money; because no one can forecast every year individually forever, analysts typically project cash flows for five or ten years and then add a terminal value, a single figure representing all cash flows beyond the forecast period, usually calculated by assuming steady growth at some rate.

In practice, the terminal value often accounts for well over half, and for fast-growing companies frequently the large majority, of the total valuation, which means that the result depends heavily on two assumptions about the distant future: the long-run growth rate and the discount rate. Small changes in either can move the valuation dramatically. If the discount rate is nine per cent, assuming perpetual growth of three rather than two per cent raises the terminal value by roughly a sixth; narrowing the gap further produces even larger swings, and a growth rate approaching the discount rate makes the formula explode.

The model is still useful, because it forces explicit assumptions about cash, growth and risk rather than relying on multiples or sentiment, but its precision is often illusory. Good practice includes testing how the valuation responds to a range of assumptions, checking whether the implied terminal growth is plausible relative to the economy, and asking what must be true about the business’s competitive position for its profits to persist that long. A valuation is better read as a structured argument about the future than as a measurement of a fact.
g: DCF values a company by discounting forecast cash, adding a terminal value for all years beyond the forecast.
Terminal value often dominates, so the long-run growth and discount rate assumptions swing results dramatically, even exploding near each other.

passages.t: The bar that investments must clear
passages.q: Why do companies often demand higher returns than their cost of capital?
p: Finance textbooks teach that a company should invest in any project whose expected return exceeds its cost of capital, usually measured as the weighted average cost of capital, a blend of the returns required by lenders and shareholders; projects that clear this bar create value, and rejecting them leaves value on the table. Yet surveys of chief financial officers have found that many firms set hurdle rates, the minimum return they require, well above their estimated cost of capital, sometimes by several percentage points.

Research by Ravi Jagannathan and colleagues, published in 2016, suggested reasons. Managers know that project forecasts tend to be optimistic, so a higher hurdle builds in a margin of safety. Companies also face constraints that the textbook model ignores: limited managerial attention and organisational capacity mean that a firm cannot pursue every project that clears the cost of capital, so it effectively rations opportunities, and a higher hurdle selects the best. Firms with fewer constraints were found to set hurdles closer to their cost of capital.

The practice is sensible in moderation but has costs. A hurdle set too high causes a company to underinvest, passing up projects that would have created value and potentially ceding ground to competitors with lower thresholds, while a single uniform hurdle applied to projects of very different risk can favour risky projects in safe businesses and reject safe ones in risky businesses. Better practice adjusts the required return for each project’s actual risk and addresses forecast optimism directly, through reviews of past projections against outcomes, rather than relying on an inflated bar to do the work.
g: Textbooks say invest whenever returns beat the cost of capital, but surveys show firms set hurdles well above it.

passages.t: Preparing for futures you cannot predict
passages.q: How can planning help when the future is genuinely uncertain?
p: In the early 1970s a team at Royal Dutch Shell led by Pierre Wack developed scenario planning, not to predict the future but to prepare managers for several plausible futures that differed in ways that mattered. One scenario they explored was that oil-producing countries might assert control over supply and drive prices sharply higher, a possibility most of the industry regarded as remote; when the oil shock of 1973 arrived, Shell is widely reported to have adapted faster than many competitors because its managers had already rehearsed the implications.

Scenarios differ from forecasts in purpose and form. A forecast offers a single expected outcome with error bars; scenarios describe a small number of internally consistent stories built around the most important and uncertain drivers, such as technology, regulation or geopolitics, each sufficiently different to challenge assumptions. Their value lies less in their accuracy than in changing how decision-makers perceive signals: managers who have imagined a future in detail are more likely to recognise its early signs and less likely to dismiss them.

Scenario planning can be misused as an elaborate exercise that produces documents rather than decisions. Its practical payoff comes when organisations identify strategies that perform reasonably well across several scenarios, prepare options that can be activated if a particular future begins to unfold, and agree in advance on the signposts that would indicate which scenario is emerging. Used this way, it turns uncertainty from a reason for paralysis into a basis for preparation.
g: Shell’s Wack developed scenario planning to prepare for several plausible futures, and it reportedly adapted faster to the 1973 oil shock.
Scenarios are a few consistent stories around key uncertain drivers rather than single forecasts, and they help managers recognise early signals.

passages.q: How can goal-setting align a large organisation without micromanaging it?
p: The goal-setting method known as objectives and key results was developed at Intel under Andy Grove in the 1970s and carried to Google in 1999 by the investor John Doerr, who later popularised it widely. An objective states qualitatively what an organisation or team wants to achieve; a small number of key results specify measurably how progress will be judged, so that a team can tell, at the end of a period, whether it got there, and objectives are typically shared openly so that teams can see how their goals connect.

The approach draws on decades of research by the psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham, which found that specific, challenging goals tend to produce higher performance than vague exhortations to do one’s best, provided people are committed to the goals and receive feedback. Practitioners often recommend setting some goals ambitious enough that achieving seventy per cent of them counts as success, to encourage stretch rather than safe targets.

The method fails in recognisable ways. When key results are tied directly to pay, teams tend to set targets they know they can hit, defeating the purpose; when they multiply, they become a bureaucratic exercise that consumes time without focusing effort; and when key results measure activity, such as the number of meetings held, rather than outcomes, they reward motion over progress. Like any metric, key results are susceptible to gaming, and their value depends less on the template than on honest conversations about what matters most.
g: OKRs came from Intel under Grove and reached Google via Doerr, pairing a qualitative objective with measurable key results shared openly.

passages.t: Who pays on a two-sided platform?
passages.q: Why do platforms often charge one side nothing and the other side a lot?
p: A payment card network serves two groups: cardholders, who want to pay wherever they shop, and merchants, who want to accept the cards their customers carry. Each group values the platform more when the other is large, and the platform’s pricing problem is therefore unusual: it must decide not only how much to charge overall but how to divide charges between the sides. The economists Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole formalised this problem in work for which Tirole received the 2014 Nobel Prize, alongside his broader work on market power.

Their analysis showed that the profit-maximising and even the socially efficient structure can involve charging one side far below cost, sometimes negative, if that side is more sensitive to price and its participation makes the platform much more valuable to the other side. Card networks have historically charged merchants fees while offering cardholders rewards; video game console makers have often sold consoles at low margins and earned money from game developers; dating apps have at times admitted some users free. Low prices on one side are not charity but a means of attracting the participants that make the other side willing to pay.

The framework complicates competition policy. A price below cost on one side might look like predatory pricing in an ordinary market but be a normal feature of a two-sided one, while high fees on the other side might reflect market power or simply the structure of the platform. Regulators have sometimes capped fees, as the European Union did for card interchange fees in 2015, and the debate over where such interventions help or harm continues. Analysing any platform requires looking at both sides together rather than either in isolation.
g: Card networks serve cardholders and merchants who each value the other’s size, so platforms must split charges, which Rochet and Tirole formalised.
Optimal structures may charge the price-sensitive, valuable side below cost, as with card rewards, cheap consoles and free dating users.

passages.q: Why do industries swing between bundling products together and splitting them apart?
p: The technology executive Jim Barksdale is often credited with the remark that there are only two ways to make money in business, bundling and unbundling, and the history of media and software lends it some support. Cable television bundled hundreds of channels into a single subscription; streaming services unbundled them; and as streaming fragmented into many services, aggregators and bundles began to reappear. Newspapers bundled news, classified advertising and entertainment, until the internet unbundled each into specialised sites.

Bundling can be valuable for both sellers and buyers. Because customers value different components differently, a bundle priced at their combined average willingness to pay can capture more revenue than selling each item separately, while giving buyers access to items they would not have purchased individually. Bundles also reduce transaction costs and can deter competitors, since a rival selling one component must compete against a package. Software suites, in which several applications are sold together, have long exploited these economics.

Unbundling becomes attractive when technology lowers the cost of distributing components separately, when customers resent paying for parts they never use, or when specialised competitors can serve one component far better than the bundle does. The cycle tends to repeat because unbundled offerings eventually overwhelm customers with choice and payments, creating demand for a new aggregator. Strategists can therefore ask, of any market, whether the current structure leaves customers paying for unwanted parts or managing too many fragments, since either condition signals that the next shift may be near.
g: Barksdale said money is made by bundling and unbundling, which media history shows as cable, streaming and newspapers swung back and forth.
Bundles capture more revenue across varied valuations, cut transaction costs and deter rivals, as software suites show.
Unbundling wins when distribution gets cheaper or specialists excel, and fragmentation later revives bundles, so look for the next shift.
k: Industries cycle between bundling and unbundling (cable → streaming → new bundles; newspapers → specialised sites).

passages.q: Which stages of a value chain capture the most profit?
p: Michael Porter’s 1985 concept of the value chain describes a company’s activities, from inbound logistics and operations to marketing, sales and service, as a sequence in which value is added at each step, and he argued that competitive advantage comes from performing particular activities more cheaply or distinctively than rivals. Extended across an industry, the idea prompts a related question: which stages of the overall chain, from components to final customer, capture the most profit?

In 1992 Stan Shih, the founder of the Taiwanese computer company Acer, proposed an answer for the personal computer industry, which he illustrated as a smile curve: value added and margins were highest at the two ends of the chain, in research, design and key components on one side and in brands, distribution and services on the other, while assembly and manufacturing in the middle, though essential, were commoditised and earned thin margins. The image has since been applied to many industries in which production became widely available.

The curve is not a law, and it can shift. Some manufacturing, such as advanced semiconductor fabrication, has become so difficult and capital-intensive that it commands high margins, and firms like TSMC capture substantial value in the supposedly low-margin middle. The useful question for strategists is not which stages are inherently profitable but where in their own industry scarce capabilities, bargaining power and differentiation currently sit, and whether that distribution is stable or about to change.
g: Porter’s value chain sees advantage in doing particular activities better, which raises the question of which industry stages earn most.

passages.q: Which sources of competitive advantage tend to last?
p: Warren Buffett popularised the metaphor of an economic moat, a durable advantage that protects a business’s profits from competitors in the way a moat protects a castle, and analysts at the research firm Morningstar developed a widely used classification of its sources: intangible assets such as brands, patents and licences; switching costs; network effects; cost advantages arising from scale, location or processes; and efficient scale, in which a market is only large enough to support a few profitable firms, deterring new entrants.

The distinction between a moat and a mere competitive edge is durability. A superior product, a talented management team or a successful marketing campaign may produce excellent results for a time, but if competitors can copy them, returns will tend to fall towards average as rivals invest. A moat exists only when there is a structural reason that competitors cannot replicate the advantage at a reasonable cost, and the evidence for it is returns on capital that remain high over many years despite attempts to compete.

Moats can erode, sometimes quickly. Technological change can make a cost advantage irrelevant, regulation can open protected markets, and network effects can unravel if users migrate to a new platform. Analysts therefore ask not only whether a moat exists but whether it is widening or narrowing, and executives inside a company can ask the same: which of our advantages would a well-funded rival struggle to copy in five years, and are we investing to deepen those, or merely to defend results that rest on something easier to imitate?
g: Buffett’s moat is a durable advantage, and Morningstar classifies sources as intangibles, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages and efficient scale.
A moat differs from an edge by durability, needing a structural reason rivals cannot copy, shown by persistently high returns.
Moats erode through technology, regulation or migration, so ask whether yours is widening and what a rival could not copy in five years.
k: Moat sources: intangibles, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, efficient scale.
A moat is a structural, durable advantage; evidence is sustained high returns on capital.

passages.t: Creative tools in the age of generative AI
passages.q: How should an established creative software company respond to AI that can generate images and video?
p: The arrival of generative models able to produce images, video and designs from text prompts presented incumbent creative software firms with a classic dilemma: the technology threatened to commoditise some tasks their products had long served, such as producing stock imagery or simple edits, while also offering a way to make their tools more powerful. Start-ups and large technology companies released image generators at remarkable speed, and some observers predicted that professional creative tools would be displaced.

Adobe’s response illustrates one strategic path. In 2023 it launched Firefly, a family of generative models that it said had been trained on licensed content, including its own stock library, and public-domain material, positioning them as safer for commercial use than models trained on scraped images of uncertain provenance, and it embedded generation directly in existing applications such as Photoshop, so that AI features augmented established workflows rather than replacing them. The approach sought to turn the incumbent’s assets, a vast installed base of professional users, licensed content and integration across tools, into advantages in the new technology.

Whether such strategies succeed depends on questions still unresolved: whether professionals will continue to value fine-grained control and integration over the speed of standalone generators, how intellectual-property law around training data will settle, how quickly rival models improve, and whether the value of creative work shifts from execution towards direction and taste. The case is a live example of the innovator’s dilemma in which the incumbent is attempting the hardest response: embracing the disruptive technology quickly enough to shape it without abandoning the customers and economics on which it depends.
g: Generative AI threatened to commoditise some creative tasks while offering to strengthen incumbents’ tools, and some predicted displacement.
Adobe launched Firefly trained on licensed and public-domain content and embedded it in existing apps, turning incumbent assets into AI advantages.
Success depends on user preferences, IP law, rival progress and shifting value of creative work, making it a live innovator’s dilemma.

passages.q: How can a platform enter a neighbouring market and win with little effort?
p: The strategy scholars Thomas Eisenmann, Geoffrey Parker and Marshall Van Alstyne described in 2011 a pattern they called platform envelopment: a provider in one platform market enters another by bundling its own functionality with that of the target market, leveraging shared users and relationships so that the combined offering is more attractive than a standalone rival, even if the rival’s product is better on its own terms.

Because the attacker already reaches a large base of users, it can offer the new function at little or no extra charge, absorbing the costs across its existing business, while the specialist must charge for its product and persuade users to adopt something separate. Historical examples include operating systems absorbing functions such as web browsing and media playback that independent companies had sold, and office software suites incorporating video calling and collaboration tools that once required separate products.

For specialists, the threat suggests defensive strategies: building network effects and switching costs of their own before an adjacent platform arrives, becoming a platform themselves by attracting complementary products, forming alliances, or focusing on segments where depth of functionality matters more than convenience. For competition authorities, envelopment raises difficult questions, since bundling can deliver genuine convenience to users while also extending dominance from one market into another, which is why such cases, from Microsoft in the 1990s onwards, have been among the most contested in antitrust history.
g: Eisenmann, Parker and Van Alstyne described platform envelopment: a platform bundles a neighbouring market’s function using shared users.
Attackers can offer the function nearly free across their base while specialists must charge, as with browsers and office video calling.
Specialists should build their own networks, platforms or alliances, and regulators struggle since bundling helps users yet extends dominance.

Attackers spread costs and offer features free; specialists must charge (browsers, media players, video calls).

passages.q: How can giving most users a product for free be profitable?
p: In a freemium model, a company offers a basic version of its product at no charge and sells premium features, capacity or support to a minority of users; the free tier serves as marketing and distribution, attracting users who might never have tried a paid product, some of whom later convert to paying customers. Software, games, music streaming and cloud storage have all used the model extensively.

Conversion rates are typically low, often in the low single digits as a percentage of free users, which means that the economics depend on a delicate balance. The cost of serving each free user must be small, since the many who never pay are subsidised by the few who do; the free version must be valuable enough to attract and retain users but limited enough that serious users have reasons to upgrade; and the value of each paying customer over their lifetime must cover the costs of serving and acquiring the free base from which they came. Products whose free users also add value, by creating content or inviting colleagues, can make the model particularly powerful.

Freemium fails when the free tier is so generous that few need to upgrade, when free users are expensive to serve, as with storage or computing-heavy products, or when the line between free and paid feels arbitrary and breeds resentment. A common refinement is to align paid tiers with the moments when users derive more value, such as working in teams, handling larger projects or using a product for business, so that upgrading feels like a natural step rather than a toll.
g: Freemium gives a basic product free and sells premium features to a minority, using the free tier as distribution.
Conversion is usually low single digits, so free users must be cheap, the free tier useful but limited, and payers worth enough to cover the base.
It fails when free is too generous or costly or the line feels arbitrary, so align paid tiers with moments of greater value.

passages.q: When should a company rely on its product, rather than salespeople, to win customers?
p: Traditional enterprise software was sold top-down: sales teams cultivated executives, negotiated large contracts and only then rolled the product out to employees who had little say in the choice. Over the past two decades, many software companies, from collaboration tools to developer platforms, have instead grown through what is now called product-led growth, in which individual users discover, try and adopt a product themselves, often for free, and the organisation pays later once usage has spread.

The approach can be highly efficient. Acquisition costs fall because the product itself does much of the marketing, through ease of adoption, invitations to colleagues and visible value; feedback from real usage arrives quickly and shapes development; and expansion within an organisation can follow naturally as more teams adopt the tool. Companies that grew this way have often reached large revenues with sales costs well below those of traditional vendors.

Product-led growth is not a universal solution. Complex products requiring integration, security review or organisational change still need skilled sellers, and large customers often want negotiated terms and support that self-service cannot provide. Many successful companies therefore combine the two, letting product-led adoption create demand inside organisations and deploying sales teams to convert widespread usage into enterprise agreements, a hybrid sometimes called product-led sales. The strategic question is which motion fits the product’s complexity, price and buyer, and how the two should hand off to each other.
g: Enterprise software was sold top-down by sales teams, but many firms now grow product-led as users adopt first and organisations pay later.
It is efficient because the product markets itself, feedback is fast and usage spreads, so sales costs are low.

k: Top-down sales versus product-led growth, where users adopt first and organisations pay later.
Product-led growth lowers acquisition costs, speeds feedback and expands naturally.

passages.q: How do investors judge whether a fast-growing software company is healthy?
p: Investors in software companies face a recurring dilemma: rapid growth usually requires heavy spending on sales, marketing and development that depresses profits, while profitable companies may be growing slowly. A simple heuristic known as the rule of forty attempts to balance the two by adding a company’s revenue growth rate to its profit margin, often measured as operating cash flow or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and treating a combined figure above forty per cent as a sign of a healthy business.

The rule allows companies to be compared across different stages. A firm growing at sixty per cent with a loss margin of twenty per cent scores forty, as does one growing at ten per cent with a margin of thirty; both, on the heuristic, are balancing growth and efficiency acceptably. Studies by investment firms have found that companies scoring above the threshold have, on average, commanded higher valuation multiples, which helps explain why executives and boards track it closely.

Like any single metric, the rule simplifies too much to be a target in itself. It treats a point of growth as equivalent to a point of margin, which may not reflect their relative value at different scales; it can be flattered by the choice of profit measure, since excluding certain costs, such as share-based pay, raises margins; and it says nothing about the durability of either growth or margins. It is best used as a quick screen that prompts deeper questions about where growth comes from and whether margins will expand as the company scales.
g: Software investors trade off growth and profit, so the rule of forty adds growth rate to margin and treats over 40% as healthy.

passages.q: Why can limiting your own options strengthen your position?
p: The economist Thomas Schelling, in The Strategy of Conflict, published in 1960, observed that in bargaining and conflict, the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself: a negotiator who can credibly commit to a position, by making retreat impossible or very costly, can force the other side to adjust, because threats and promises influence behaviour only if they are believed. Schelling shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this analysis of credible commitment.

History supplies dramatic, if sometimes embellished, illustrations, such as commanders said to have burned their ships after landing so that their soldiers could not retreat, signalling to themselves and their enemies that they would fight. The commercial equivalents are more mundane but similar in logic: a company that builds a large factory signals to potential entrants that it will fight for market share, since its investment cannot be recovered; a firm that publicly guarantees to match any competitor’s price makes undercutting it pointless; and a leader who announces a decision publicly raises the cost of later backing down.

Commitment is powerful only when it is credible and when the committed position is wise, since binding oneself to a poor choice simply guarantees a poor outcome. It can also escalate conflict if both sides commit to incompatible positions, leaving no room for compromise. The strategic skill lies in choosing which positions to make irreversible, how to signal them convincingly, and where to preserve flexibility, recognising that the value of keeping options open and the value of closing them depend on what one is trying to induce others to do.
g: Schelling showed you can constrain an adversary by credibly binding yourself, because threats only work if believed, earning a 2005 Nobel.
Burning boats, sunk factory investments, price-matching guarantees and public announcements all make retreat costly and credible.
Commitment needs credibility and wisdom and can escalate conflict, so choose which positions to fix and where to keep flexibility.
k: Schelling (1960): credible self-binding commitments can force others to adjust; Nobel 2005.
Examples: burning boats, irreversible factories, price-match guarantees, public announcements.

passages.q: Why do quick fixes in software and organisations become expensive later?
p: The programmer Ward Cunningham introduced the metaphor of technical debt in 1992 to explain to non-technical colleagues why rushing code out quickly could be a sensible choice that carried a future cost: shipping imperfect code is like borrowing money, allowing faster progress now in exchange for interest payments later, in the form of extra effort every time the code must be changed, until the debt is repaid by rewriting it properly.

The metaphor clarified that debt is not inherently bad; a start-up racing to test a product with customers may rationally accept it, just as a company may borrow to fund growth. The problem arises when debt is accumulated unknowingly or never repaid. Interest compounds: each workaround makes the next change harder, systems become fragile, engineers spend increasing time maintaining rather than building, and eventually even small changes become slow and risky. Surveys of developers consistently report substantial portions of their time lost to such maintenance.

Organisations accumulate analogous debt outside software: processes patched rather than redesigned, roles defined around individuals who have left, reporting lines created for problems long solved and policies layered on policies. Like technical debt, organisational debt is invisible in quarterly results but surfaces as slowness, confusion and difficulty changing direction. Managing it well means making debt deliberate rather than accidental, recording where it has been taken on, and setting aside regular capacity to repay it before the interest overwhelms the principal.
g: Cunningham’s technical debt metaphor says rushed code is like borrowing: faster now, with interest paid later in extra effort.
Debt can be rational, but unknown or unpaid debt compounds into fragile systems and lost time, as developer surveys show.

passages.q: Should companies be run mainly for shareholders or for a wider set of stakeholders?
p: In a widely discussed essay of 1970, the economist Milton Friedman argued that a company’s social responsibility is to make as much profit as it can while staying within the law and competing honestly; executives who spend shareholders’ money on social causes, he argued, are in effect imposing taxes without accountability, and social goals are better pursued by individuals and governments.

The shareholder view dominated much of corporate governance in the following decades, reinforced by pay tied to share prices. Critics argued that it encouraged short-termism and neglected employees, communities and the environment, and in 2019 the Business Roundtable, an association of large American companies, issued a statement redefining the purpose of a corporation to include commitments to all its stakeholders, customers, employees, suppliers and communities, as well as shareholders. Sceptics questioned whether the statement changed behaviour, and some argued that serving everyone means being accountable to no one.

The positions may be less opposed than they appear. Most shareholder-oriented thinkers accept that long-term value depends on treating employees, customers and suppliers well, while most stakeholder advocates accept that a company must remain profitable to serve anyone. The practical disagreements concern trade-offs where interests genuinely conflict, who decides how they are weighed, and how managers are held to account, questions that are answered as much by law, ownership and incentives as by statements of purpose.
g: Friedman argued in 1970 that business should increase profits within the rules, leaving social goals to individuals and governments.
Shareholder primacy dominated, but critics cited short-termism, and the 2019 Business Roundtable statement embraced stakeholders, though sceptics doubted its effect.
The views overlap on long-term value, so real disputes are about conflicting trade-offs, who decides and accountability.

passages.q: What did the case against Microsoft reveal about dominance in technology?
p: In 1998 the United States Department of Justice and a group of states sued Microsoft, alleging that the company had used its monopoly in personal computer operating systems to crush competition in web browsers, most notably by bundling its Internet Explorer browser with Windows and pressuring computer makers and internet providers to favour it over Netscape Navigator. The government argued that browsers threatened to become a platform on which applications could run regardless of operating system, eroding the barrier that protected Windows.

In 2000 a district judge ruled that Microsoft had violated antitrust law and ordered it to be split into two companies. An appeals court in 2001 upheld much of the finding that Microsoft had illegally maintained its monopoly but overturned the break-up order, and the case was settled with restrictions on Microsoft’s conduct, including requirements to share certain technical information with rivals. By then, Netscape had lost most of its share of the browser market.

Assessments of the case diverge. Some argue that the constraints and scrutiny it imposed made Microsoft more cautious in the following decade, leaving room for new firms, including Google, to grow without being smothered; others contend that market forces, not litigation, eroded Microsoft’s dominance as computing moved to the web and mobile devices. The case set a template for later actions against large technology companies, centred on the question of when bundling and exclusive arrangements serve users and when they illegitimately extend a monopoly into new markets.
g: In 1998 the US sued Microsoft for using its Windows monopoly to crush Netscape by bundling and pressure, fearing browsers would erode Windows.

passages.q: How did a company that designs no chips of its own become indispensable to the industry?
p: When Morris Chang founded Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company in 1987, the prevailing model in the chip industry was vertical integration: companies such as Intel designed chips and manufactured them in their own fabrication plants. Chang’s idea was a pure-play foundry, a manufacturer that would make chips designed by others and never compete with its customers by selling chips of its own, removing the risk that a customer’s designs would be copied by a rival.

The model enabled a new kind of company: the fabless chip designer, which could create advanced products without the billions of dollars needed to build fabrication plants. Firms such as Nvidia, Qualcomm and later Apple, designing its own processors, could concentrate on design while TSMC concentrated on the formidably difficult task of manufacturing at ever smaller scales. Because each new generation of manufacturing technology costs more to develop, aggregating demand from many customers allowed TSMC to invest at a scale few integrated rivals could match, and it pulled ahead at the leading edge.

The result has been an unusual concentration of strategic importance. A large share of the world’s most advanced chips, used in smartphones, data centres and artificial intelligence, are manufactured by a single company, much of it on an island at the centre of geopolitical tension. Governments in the United States, Europe and Asia have responded with large subsidies to build domestic manufacturing, including TSMC plants abroad. The story illustrates how specialisation can create both extraordinary efficiency and new forms of systemic risk.
g: Morris Chang founded TSMC in 1987 as a pure-play foundry that makes others’ chips and never competes with customers.
This enabled fabless designers like Nvidia, Qualcomm and Apple, and aggregating demand let TSMC outinvest rivals at the leading edge.
Advanced chipmaking is now concentrated in one company on a geopolitically tense island, so governments subsidise domestic plants, showing specialisation’s risk.
k: TSMC (1987) pioneered the pure-play foundry model, never competing with its customers.

passages.q: How should the speed of a decision depend on whether it can be undone?
p: In his 2015 letter to shareholders, Amazon’s founder Jeff Bezos distinguished between two types of decision. A minority carry heavy consequences and are hard or impossible to undo, which he likened to one-way doors; these should be made methodically and slowly, with wide consultation. The majority can be reversed, two-way doors in his phrase, so a suboptimal choice of this kind is not a lasting sentence: if it proves wrong, the organisation can simply step back and choose again.

Bezos warned that growing organisations drift into treating every decision as if it were a one-way door, wrapping reversible choices in heavyweight process, and that the result is a company that moves slowly, avoids sensible risks, runs too few experiments and, in the end, invents less. Small, quick, reversible decisions, he argued, should be made by high-judgement individuals or small groups without lengthy approval, because the cost of being slow often exceeds the cost of occasionally being wrong.

The distinction is a practical tool for any executive. Before deciding, it helps to ask how costly it would be to reverse the choice and how quickly one would learn whether it was right; where reversal is cheap and learning is fast, deciding quickly and adjusting is usually wiser than analysing at length. The difficulty lies in classifying decisions correctly, since some that appear reversible, such as a product launch or a public announcement, carry reputational or organisational costs that make them harder to undo than they look.
g: Bezos distinguished irreversible one-way-door decisions, which need careful deliberation, from reversible two-way doors, which can be undone.
Growing firms apply heavy process to every decision, causing slowness and less invention, so reversible decisions should be made quickly by small groups.
So ask how costly reversal is and how fast you will learn, but classify carefully, since some decisions are harder to undo than they look.
k: One-way doors (irreversible) deserve slow, careful decisions; two-way doors (reversible) can be made quickly (Bezos, 2015).
Applying heavy process to every decision causes slowness, risk aversion and less invention.
Ask how costly reversal is and how fast you’ll learn; beware decisions that look reversible but aren’t.

passages.q: Should a new product launch at a high price or a low one?
p: Companies launching new products often choose between two broad pricing strategies. Price skimming sets a high initial price to capture customers willing to pay a premium, such as enthusiasts and early adopters, then lowers it over time to reach more price-sensitive buyers; penetration pricing sets a low initial price to win market share quickly, build a user base and establish the product before competitors arrive, with the intention of raising prices or profiting from scale later.

Each fits different conditions. Skimming suits products with strong differentiation, protection from imitation, such as patents, and a customer base with widely varying willingness to pay, and it allows a company to recover development costs quickly; consumer electronics and new pharmaceuticals have often followed this path. Penetration suits markets with network effects, high switching costs or significant economies of scale, where early share brings lasting advantages, and where competitors could enter quickly if prices left room for them.

Both carry risks. Skimming can invite competitors attracted by high margins and can frustrate early buyers who see prices fall soon after purchase. Penetration can anchor customers on a low price that is hard to raise without backlash, attract customers who leave when prices rise, and burn cash if the expected scale or lock-in fails to materialise. The choice should rest on an honest assessment of how quickly rivals can imitate, how much early share is truly worth, and how customers will react to later price changes.
g: Firms choose skimming, which starts high and lowers prices, or penetration, which starts low to win share.
Skimming suits differentiated, protected products with varied willingness to pay, while penetration suits network effects, switching costs and scale.
Skimming invites rivals and frustrates early buyers, penetration anchors low prices and burns cash, so judge imitation, share value and reactions.
k: Skimming: start high, lower over time; penetration: start low to win share.
Skimming fits differentiated, protected products; penetration fits network effects, switching costs and scale.
